definition: The regulation of the internal conditions of the body to maintain a stable environment for cells to function optimally.
The conditions inside the body, including temperature, blood glucose, water and ion levels, that need to be kept within narrow limits.
A control mechanism where a change from the normal level triggers a response that reverses the change and returns conditions to normal.
A cell or organ that detects a change in the environment (a stimulus) and sends a signal to a coordinator.
The brain or spinal cord — processes information from receptors and organises a response.
A muscle or gland that carries out the response to a stimulus.
A specialised cell that transmits electrical impulses around the nervous system.
A nerve cell that carries electrical impulses from receptors to the central nervous system.
A nerve cell that carries electrical impulses from the central nervous system to effectors (muscles or glands).
A nerve cell found in the brain and spinal cord that connects sensory neurones to motor neurones.
The tiny gap between two neurones where a chemical neurotransmitter carries the signal from one neurone to the next.
A chemical released at a synapse that diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the next neurone to transmit the signal.
A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought, coordinated by the spinal cord.
The pathway taken by a nerve impulse during a reflex action: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector.
The brain and spinal cord — the coordinator of the nervous system.
The system of glands that produce and secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
A chemical messenger produced by a gland, released into the blood and carried to target organs where it causes a response.
An organ that produces and secretes substances — endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the blood.
The master gland in the brain that produces many hormones controlling other glands, including FSH and LH.
A gland that produces insulin and glucagon to regulate blood glucose concentration.
A hormone produced by the pancreas that causes cells to absorb glucose from the blood, lowering blood glucose concentration.
A hormone produced by the pancreas that causes the liver to convert glycogen back to glucose, raising blood glucose concentration.
An insoluble carbohydrate stored in the liver and muscles, made from glucose when blood glucose is too high.
A condition where the pancreas does not produce enough insulin, causing blood glucose levels to become dangerously high. Treated with insulin injections.
A condition where body cells no longer respond to insulin properly. Associated with obesity and treated with diet and exercise.
The process by which the body maintains a constant core temperature of approximately 37°C.
The region of the brain that monitors blood temperature and coordinates the body's response to changes in temperature.
The widening of blood vessels near the skin surface to increase heat loss from the body when too hot.
The narrowing of blood vessels near the skin surface to reduce heat loss from the body when too cold.
The production of sweat by sweat glands in the skin. As sweat evaporates it transfers heat energy away from the body, cooling it down.
Rapid involuntary muscle contractions that generate heat to warm the body when core temperature drops.
A female sex hormone produced by the ovaries that causes development of secondary sexual characteristics and controls the menstrual cycle.
The main male sex hormone produced by the testes that causes development of secondary sexual characteristics.
Follicle stimulating hormone — produced by the pituitary gland, causes eggs to mature in the ovaries and stimulates oestrogen production.
Luteinising hormone — produced by the pituitary gland, triggers ovulation (the release of a mature egg).
A hormone that maintains the uterus lining during pregnancy and is used in some contraceptives.
In vitro fertilisation — a fertility treatment where eggs are fertilised outside the body and implanted into the uterus.
Methods used to prevent pregnancy, including hormonal methods (pill, injection) and non-hormonal methods (condom, barrier methods).
A hormone produced by the adrenal glands in response to stress or danger, preparing the body for 'fight or flight'.
A hormone produced by the thyroid gland that regulates the metabolic rate of the body.
